opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to let kids treat AI as a collaborator on something *they* actually care about, rather than as a homework machine. The real value isn't getting the answer faster. It's that a kid with a real interest, say building a game, designing a robot, or writing a story set in a world they invented, can now go much further than they could alone. AI lowers the floor on getting started and raises the ceiling on what's achievable.

When I think about how kids learn best, it's through agency: you pick a goal, you try something, it doesn't work, you figure out why, and you try again. AI can be wonderful in that loop. It can explain a concept at exactly the level you need, right when you need it. It can unblock you when you're stuck on some piece of syntax that would otherwise make an eleven-year-old give up. It can be the patient tutor who never gets tired of "but why?"

The risk is the opposite: the AI does the thinking and the kid just watches. So I'd encourage parents and teachers to focus less on whether kids are "using AI" and more on whether the kid is the one making decisions. Are they choosing what to build? Can they explain why it works? When the AI gives them something, do they question it, test it, and change it? Those habits, taste, judgment, and the ability to direct a very capable tool toward your own goals, are going to be the core skills going forward.

And honestly, the projects should be ambitious. Kids today can attempt things that used to require a team of adults. I'd rather a kid aim at something too big, use AI to get surprisingly far, and learn a ton from where it breaks, than do a small safe project that the AI could have finished on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says children should use AI as a collaborator on projects they care about and emphasizes that the child should choose goals and make decisions.

r002.rationale: It warns that AI doing the thinking can leave a child watching, but does not specifically say that AI producing code can undermine a child’s willingness to learn programming.

r003.rationale: It describes AI explaining concepts as needed, but does not recommend learning a task’s basics before using AI to extend one’s capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing is that kids should treat AI as a collaborator on something they actually care about, not as a shortcut to avoid thinking. The magic of a project is that you own it. You pick the goal, you hit walls, you figure out how to get past them. AI is incredible at helping with that last part, but it shouldn't take away the first two.

So the way I'd frame it for a kid is: you're the one driving. You decide you want to build a game, or write a story, or figure out how a rocket works. Then the AI becomes this infinitely patient tutor that will explain anything, at whatever level you need, as many times as you want. That's genuinely new. When I was growing up, if you got stuck on something and nobody around you knew the answer, you were just stuck. Now you can ask, and keep asking until it clicks.

The thing I'd be careful about is the moment where the AI just does the whole thing for you. If a kid asks "write me a game" and gets a working game back, they've learned almost nothing. But if they ask "why does my character fall through the floor" and the AI walks them through collision detection, they've learned something real and they still have the pride of having built it themselves. The difference is whether the struggle gets removed or whether it gets supported.

And honestly, I think parents and teachers have a role in shaping that. Encourage kids to ask the AI to explain rather than to produce. Encourage them to argue with it, to check whether it's right. Models still make mistakes, and catching those mistakes is one of the best ways to actually learn the material. A kid who gets in the habit of saying "wait, that doesn't seem right, let me verify" is going to be in great shape no matter what the technology looks like in ten years.

The bigger picture is that the skills that matter are shifting. Memorizing facts matters less. Knowing what question to ask, having taste about what's worth building, being able to tell good output from bad output, those matter more. Projects are the best way to develop that, and AI makes it possible for a ten-year-old to take on projects that would have been out of reach before. That's the part I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response says children should own the project, choose what to build, and drive the work, with AI supporting them.

r002.rationale: It warns that having AI make the whole game means the child learns little and removes the struggle, but does not clearly say this can undermine the child’s willingness to learn.

r003.rationale: It encourages using AI to explain and support projects, but does not recommend understanding a task’s basics before using AI to extend one’s capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing is that AI can shorten the distance between a child having an idea and being able to try it. If you want to make a game or write a story, you can get help with the parts you don’t know how to do yet. That gives you a reason to learn: there’s something you actually want to build.

But I’d want the child to stay in charge of the project. What are you trying to make? Why did you choose that approach? How would you tell whether it works? The AI can offer hints, explain something, or help you get unstuck, while you still make those decisions.

And sometimes you should put it aside and see what you can do yourself. Getting a working result is exciting, but you also want to come away understanding more than you did when you started.

r001.rationale: The response says the child should stay in charge of their own project and make the key decisions, with AI offering support.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that AI producing code can undermine a child's willingness to do the work of learning programming.

r003.rationale: It encourages children to understand more and sometimes work without AI, but does not recommend learning a task's basics before using AI to extend their capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most exciting use is helping kids pursue something they actually want to make. If you want to build a game, write a story, or understand how a robot works, AI can help you get past obstacles that might otherwise stop you.

But you want the child to stay in charge of the project. Instead of just asking for the answer, ask for a hint, or an explanation, or a way to test your idea. Then try it yourself. The important thing is developing the confidence to say, “I have an idea, and I can figure out how to make it real.” AI can make that process much more accessible, as long as it leaves room for the child to struggle, make decisions, and discover things.

r001.rationale: It encourages children to use AI for projects they choose while keeping them in charge and making their own decisions.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking for hints rather than answers, but does not explain that AI-generated code can undermine a child's willingness to learn programming.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend learning a task's underlying basics before using AI to extend capabilities.
